items.prompt: Why does transact open with BEGIN IMMEDIATE rather than a plain BEGIN?
items.answer: It takes the write lock before the read, so two processes cannot both read and then write
distractors: IMMEDIATE commits each statement as soon as it runs, which is faster for a single JSON document update
Plain BEGIN is not supported by node:sqlite, so IMMEDIATE is the only way to open a transaction
IMMEDIATE makes the transaction read-only until the UPDATE statement runs
items.explanation: A deferred BEGIN takes its lock later, so two workers can interleave their reads; the testing guide's red-first step 2 shows the cross-process test catching exactly that.

items.prompt: A developer makes one command branch async. What does transact do, and what bug does that prevent?
items.answer: It throws and rolls back, because an async callback's writes would land after COMMIT
distractors: It awaits the returned Promise before committing, so async branches are fully supported by the store
It commits immediately and runs the async work in the background, which is safe because the document is a copy
Nothing: TypeScript already rejects async callbacks at compile time
items.explanation: The result instanceof Promise check makes the synchronous contract explicit; work that resolves after COMMIT would mutate a document that is no longer being written.

items.prompt: Alice and Bob both load an idea at version 3. Alice saves first. Writes are already serialized by BEGIN IMMEDIATE, so why is a version check still needed for Bob's save?
items.answer: Serializing writes does not detect that Bob edited stale content; comparing his captured version 3 with the current version 4 is what rejects the overwrite
distractors: Because BEGIN IMMEDIATE only serializes writes within one process
Because SQLite would otherwise merge the two titles character by character
It is not needed; the version check only exists to count edits for the audit log
items.explanation: Optimistic concurrency solves a different problem from atomicity: both users read before either transaction starts, so only the expected-version comparison inside the transaction catches the lost update.

items.prompt: In editPost, what makes the expected(p, cmd.version) call a real check rather than a display of the version?
items.answer: It checks the record as it exists inside the transaction, before touch() bumps the version
distractors: It re-fetches the current version from the browser form just before saving, so it is always up to date
It runs in the client form before the request is sent, which blocks stale saves without a server round trip
It compares cmd.version with the version stored in the session cookie
items.explanation: The page's copy may be stale; expected runs on the current record within the transaction. Do not replace the captured version with a freshly fetched one, which would approve an unreviewed overwrite.

items.prompt: A flaky network makes the client send { action: 'vote', enabled: true } twice. What is the final state?
items.answer: One vote: enabling inserts only when no row exists for that user and post
distractors: Two votes, because each request inserts a new row and the store has no unique check on the pair
No vote, because the second request toggles the first one off again
A 409 conflict on the second request, because vote commands carry an expected version
items.explanation: Vote and follow use desired state plus a unique user/post pair; a toggle command would add and then remove the vote on an accidental retry.

items.prompt: Why do the create-post and comment commands carry no expected version, and what weakness does that leave?
items.answer: They create new records, so there is no earlier version to be stale against; but without a request key they are not retry-safe, and a retried comment duplicates
distractors: They are desired-state commands, so they are already idempotent
They carry a version inside the session cookie instead
They are serialized by BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which also deduplicates retries
items.explanation: The solutions guide: creates are 'not stale-safe and not retry-safe'; the fix is a durable receipt keyed by actor, operation and client request id, checked in the same transaction.

items.prompt: An author tries to delete their Open idea that already has one vote. What happens?
items.answer: 409: a referenced idea cannot be deleted; a moderator should hide it
distractors: It is deleted together with its vote in one transaction, and the voter is notified
It is deleted and the vote is reassigned to the newest open idea in the same category
403, because only moderators may delete anything
items.explanation: deletePost requires the author, the expected version, status Open and no references in votes, follows, comments, flags, official updates, internal notes or merge history.

items.prompt: A moderator merges idea A into idea B, but idea C is already marked as a duplicate of A. What happens?
items.answer: 409: A is already a canonical target, so its duplicates must be merged first
distractors: The merge succeeds and C now points at A, which in turn points at B, forming a chain
The merge succeeds and C is silently re-pointed to B so that every duplicate shares one target
400, because merge only accepts posts with no votes
items.explanation: merge checks both versions, matching visibility and that no post has duplicateOfPostId === source.id before marking the source Duplicate and moving votes and follows.

items.prompt: The stale-edit test asserts the second save rejects AND that the first title is still stored. Why is the rejection assertion alone not enough?
items.answer: A command can write before it throws; only re-reading the record proves nothing changed
distractors: Because assert.rejects is flaky with async functions and can pass even when the promise resolves
Because the error message text may change between versions, which would break the regex
Because the first save might have been rejected too
items.explanation: Merely asserting an error misses accidental writes performed before the error, the most common way a 'conflict is handled' claim turns out false. Red-first: removing expected() fails exactly that second assertion.

items.prompt: Why does the vote race test start two separate Node processes instead of calling the service twice in one test?
items.answer: Only separate processes exercise the database lock; an in-memory Promise queue in one process could make sequential calls look safe without proving cross-process coordination
distractors: Because node:test cannot run two async calls concurrently
To double the test's speed on multi-core machines
Because each process needs its own session secret
items.explanation: The final state must contain one vote with all revisions accounted for; that is a stronger claim than two sequential calls in one process.

items.prompt: The board page gets an empty posts list. How should it decide which empty-state message to show?
items.answer: Use the service's guestBlocked flag for 'sign in', and otherwise distinguish 'no matches, clear filters' from 'nothing yet' by whether filters are active; never infer permission from posts.length === 0
distractors: Show 'sign in' whenever posts.length === 0, since empty lists mean no access
Check whether the categories list is empty to detect a blocked guest
Always show 'nothing here yet'; filters are a client concern
items.explanation: An authenticated user can legitimately have no matches, so the cause must come from guestBlocked and the active filters, not from the list length.

items.prompt: The JSON-aggregate store is migrated to relational tables updated in separate statements. Which guarantee does the guide say must not quietly disappear?
items.answer: The expected-version predicate must stay part of the write, alongside unique votes and audit retention
distractors: The 16 MiB document cap, which must be enforced separately on every table after the migration
BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which must wrap every SELECT so readers never see uncommitted rows
Cascading deletes from posts to audits, so that history stays consistent with the current posts
items.explanation: A migration succeeds only if the business guarantees survive; the guide also warns that cascading audit deletes would erase the history the app promises to keep.

items.front: How does the board make a status change, its audit and follower notifications atomic?
items.back: All three are mutations of one JSON document inside transact: BEGIN IMMEDIATE, read, synchronous change, validateDatabase, one UPDATE, COMMIT; any throw hits the catch and ROLLBACK, so none of them persist.

items.front: How do you make comment creation retry-safe?
items.back: Store a receipt keyed by actor + operation + client request id with a fingerprint of the normalized input and the created id; check it in the same transaction, return the earlier result on a match, reject a different fingerprint. The client must keep the key with the exact payload. A disabled button is not durable idempotency.

items.front: Why must the service, not the UI, enforce visibility before vote, follow, comment or flag?
items.back: A client can call a server action without clicking any button. getPost applies visible() (guest browsing, hidden, internal) inside the transaction and returns 404, and customer projections omit internal notes instead of hiding them with CSS.

items.front: Where should an email notification be sent relative to the transaction callback?
items.back: Not inside it: SQLite cannot roll back a network response, and async work cannot run in the synchronous callback anyway. Write a durable job with the business change and let a delivery worker consume it.
